title: When would you put a queue between these two services, and when wouldn't you?
summary: A justification question, not a trivia one — can you name the concrete need (surviving an outage, absorbing a burst) that earns a queue instead of reaching for one by reflex?

slides.markdown:
This question tests a reflex, not a fact: candidates who've read that "queues are good practice" often insert one between every pair of services, whether or not it solves anything. The interviewer is checking whether you can name the concrete need — surviving a downstream outage, absorbing a burst, decoupling deploy cadence — that actually earns a queue.

The honest answer is conditional: a queue helps exactly when the caller doesn't need a synchronous result. Get that condition backwards and you've added a moving part for nothing.

Before answering, ask: **does the caller need an immediate response, or can the work happen asynchronously?** And: **does the downstream service ever go down or slow down under load?**

Both questions probe the same thing from different angles — if the caller must have an answer right now, a queue only adds latency and a place for the answer to get lost. If the caller can move on without waiting, a queue is exactly the tool that lets the two services fail and recover independently.

**Queue it** when the caller doesn't need the result synchronously, or needs the interaction to survive downstream being slow or down. **Skip the queue** when the caller's very next step depends on the result — there, a queue just delays an answer the caller was going to block on anyway.

Say this out loud early: it signals you're choosing a queue for a reason, not decorating the design with one because it looks distributed-systems-y.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: checkout — inventory check vs. confirmation email
slides.markdown:
A single checkout flow contains both cases side by side.

| Step | Caller needs result now? | Queue it? |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory check | Yes — can't show "in stock" without it | No — call it synchronously |
| Order-confirmation email | No — checkout doesn't wait on the email sending | Yes — hand it to SQS and move on |

The inventory check blocks the response the user is staring at; the email doesn't. Same request, two different answers to the same question.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: what happens without the queue
slides.markdown:
Make the cost concrete: at 50,000 orders/day, the email service goes down for a 10-minute maintenance window. Without a queue, roughly 350 confirmation emails generated during that window just vanish — the synchronous call failed and nothing retained the work.

Put SQS in front of the email worker instead, and those 350 messages sit durably in the queue. The moment the worker recovers, it drains the backlog automatically — no lost emails, no manual replay.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: what the queue buys beyond outage survival
slides.markdown:
"It survives an outage" undersells it. A queue between two services also buys **independent deploy cadence** — the email worker can ship a new version without checkout even noticing — and **independent scaling**, since the worker's pool size no longer has to match checkout's request rate.

It's also a natural burst buffer: a flash sale that spikes checkout traffic 10x for five minutes doesn't require the email worker to instantly 10x too — the queue just gets a little deeper and drains at its own pace.

The happy path is one straight line. The retry-then-DLQ branch is what makes the queue actually safe in production: a message that keeps failing doesn't get lost or retried forever, it gets isolated for triage.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
A queue buys resilience and decoupling by giving up something specific: the caller's ability to know synchronously whether the work succeeded. Every hop you move behind a queue is a hop the caller can no longer get an answer about within the same request.

That's not a flaw to hide — naming it is what separates "I know queues exist" from "I understand what they cost." The next two follow-ups are exactly about paying that cost back.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how does the caller learn the async job succeeded?
slides.markdown:
If a later requirement means the caller does need to know the outcome, don't undo the queue — add a way to check back. Two standard shapes: a **status endpoint** the caller polls (`GET /jobs/{id}`), or a **webhook/callback** fired once the job finishes.

Pick polling when the caller controls the check frequency and a short delay is fine; pick a callback when the caller needs to react the moment it's done. Either way, the queue stays — you're adding an answer channel, not removing the decoupling.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: haven't you just moved the single point of failure?
slides.markdown:
A fair pushback — the queue broker is now a dependency both services share. The answer is that it's a much more available dependency: managed, clustered brokers (SQS, Amazon MSK) replicate across multiple availability zones, so the broker's own uptime is engineered to be far higher than any single service it's decoupling.

You haven't eliminated the shared dependency, you've swapped a fragile one (a specific service instance) for a durable, purpose-built one.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how much retention/buffer does the queue need?
slides.markdown:
Size retention to **the longest realistic downstream outage you want to survive**, not to an arbitrary default like "7 days because that's what the docs show."

If the email worker's worst historical outage was 40 minutes, retention comfortably above that (say, a few hours) covers real incidents without you paying for storage you'll never use. Tie the number to an actual failure mode, and you can defend it if the interviewer pushes on it.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: queuing a synchronous path and creating a polling problem
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Queues are a best practice, so I'll put one in front of the inventory check too."

**Why it's wrong:** the checkout UI can't render "in stock" or "sold out" until it has an answer. Queuing that call doesn't remove the wait — it just replaces a direct call with a poll-until-the-answer-shows-up loop, which is slower and more code for the same result.

**Correct model:** a queue removes the caller's need to wait; it doesn't help when the caller was always going to wait anyway.

Queue it when the caller doesn't need the result now, or needs the interaction to survive downstream being slow or down — skip it when the caller's next step depends on the answer. Name the trade-off (you lose a synchronous outcome) and the sizing question (retention matched to your worst realistic outage).

For the deeper mechanics of choosing between a queue and a pub/sub topic once you've decided async is right, see [queues vs pub/sub](queues-vs-pubsub).
